blocks.text: In Turkish it is simply *Kapalıçarşı*, the Covered Bazaar. Under its domes and vaults, in the old city of Istanbul, run more than sixty streets with around four thousand shops, which makes it one of the oldest and largest covered markets in the world.

Its heart is a *bedesten*: a solid stone hall under domes, with heavy gates, where valuable goods such as jewels, fine cloth and weapons were stored and traded. Sultan Mehmed II had the first one built a few years after the conquest of 1453; it was finished around 1460–1461 and is known as the *Cevahir Bedesteni*, the Jewel Bedesten, or the *İç Bedesten*, the Inner one. A second hall, the *Sandal Bedesteni*, followed; sources date it to the late 15th century or to 1545. Over time, shops grew up in the streets between and around the two halls, and the streets themselves were roofed over.

Fire was the bazaar's great enemy. It burned many times over the centuries, the last time badly in 1954, and the great Istanbul earthquake of 1894 damaged its domes. Each time it was repaired, and it is still in use today.

In the Ottoman city, each trade had its guild, and craftsmen of one trade worked side by side. The street names still show it, and they are full of the suffix `-CI` of this unit, in the plural: *Kuyumcular* (the jewellers), *Halıcılar* (the carpet sellers), *Aynacılar* (the mirror makers), *Sepetçiler* (the basket makers), *Fesçiler* (the fez makers). *Kalpakçılar Caddesi*, one of its main streets, is named after the makers of the *kalpak*, a fur hat; today it is lined with jewellers.

Today the bazaar sells gold and silver jewellery, carpets and kilims, copper pots and trays from the *bakırcılar*, the coppersmiths, leather, ceramics, lamps and souvenirs. On busy days it is said to draw a few hundred thousand visitors.

Shopping here is a conversation. Many prices are open to bargaining, *pazarlık*, and a carpet seller may offer you a glass of tea before any talk of prices. A few phrases help: *Bu ne kadar?* (How much is this?), *Biraz indirim yapar mısınız?* (Could you give me a little discount?), and, when you're only looking, *Sadece bakıyorum* (I'm just looking).

blocks.tr: Kapalıçarşı çok eski ve çok büyük bir çarşı. Çarşıda kuyumcular, halıcılar ve bakırcılar var. Sokakların adları da eski: Kuyumcular Çarşısı, Halıcılar Caddesi, Kalpakçılar Caddesi. Halıcılar müşterilere birer çay ikram eder. Sabahleyin çarşı daha sessiz. Bence burada pazarlık etmek lazım!
blocks.en: The Grand Bazaar is a very old and very big market. In the bazaar there are jewellers, carpet sellers and coppersmiths. The names of the streets are old too: the Jewellers' Market, Carpet Sellers' Street, Kalpak Makers' Street. The carpet sellers offer customers a tea each. In the morning the bazaar is quieter. I think you have to bargain here!

sources.title: Grand Bazaar, Istanbul
sources.note: Core begun in the winter of 1455/56 under Mehmed II; Cevahir (İç) Bedesten finished in 1460/61; Sandal Bedesten some years later or in 1545; 61 covered streets and over 4,000 shops; fires including 1954; the 1894 earthquake; Kalpakçılar Caddesi and Kuyumcular Çarşısı with jewellers; 250,000 to 400,000 visitors a day

sources.title: Kapalı Çarşı
sources.note: Cevahir Bedesteni from 1460–1461 under Mehmed II; Sandal Bedesteni added in 1545; more than 60 streets and about 4,000 shops; streets named after trades: Kuyumcular, Halıcılar, Aynacılar, Sepetçiler, Kalpakçılar; fires of 1546, 1651, 1710, 1730, 1750 and 1954; damage to the domes in the 1894 earthquake
